summary: The PR makes five small performance edits across requests' core files. Four of them keep the old behaviour (isascii, set lookup, removing the duplicate proxy-bypass check, and the more debatable switch to perf_counter). The apparent_encoding change only looks at the first 32 KB, which can make Response.text silently garble non-ASCII content that starts after the sample. None of the changed behaviour has new tests.

findings.title: Guessing the encoding from only the first 32 KB can silently corrupt Response.text
findings.detail: apparent_encoding now runs chardet.detect(self.content[:32768]). Response.text falls back to apparent_encoding whenever the server sends no charset, which is common. If the first 32 KB is plain ASCII and non-ASCII bytes (such as UTF-8) appear only later, the detector returns 'ascii'. text then decodes the whole body with errors='replace', so every later non-ASCII character becomes U+FFFD. No error is raised, so the data loss goes unnoticed. Large JSON or HTML responses with ASCII-only prefixes are the typical case.
findings.suggestion: Revert to detecting on self.content, or make the sample size an opt-in setting. If sampling is kept, fall back to the full body when the sample result is 'ascii' or None and len(self.content) is larger than the sample size.

findings.title: No tests for the new truncated encoding detection
findings.detail: Nothing tests that detection still works when non-ASCII content starts after the first 32 KB, or when the cut splits a multi-byte character. No test files are linked to models.py, so the regression above would not be caught.
findings.suggestion: Add a test where content is b'a'*40000 + 'é…'.encode('utf-8') repeated, with no charset header. Assert that r.text has no U+FFFD and that apparent_encoding is a UTF-8-compatible encoding. Add a second test with a multi-byte character straddling byte 32768.

findings.title: preferred_clock no longer returns wall-clock time on POSIX; comment is out of date
findings.detail: preferred_clock is a module-level name that outside code may import. On Linux and macOS it used to return epoch seconds from time.time(); it now returns perf_counter offsets with an arbitrary starting point. Using a monotonic clock for Response.elapsed is correct, but this changes what the public name returns. The comment above it still says the clock is chosen per system, which no longer applies.
findings.suggestion: Update the comment and add a changelog note that preferred_clock is now always time.perf_counter. Optionally add a test that elapsed is not affected by mocking time.time to jump.

findings.title: No tests pin resolve_proxies behaviour after the switch to getproxies()
findings.detail: resolve_proxies now calls getproxies() directly instead of get_environ_proxies(). Its behaviour is unchanged because the should_bypass_proxies guard already runs first, but no test pins that no_proxy is still honoured, the 'all' fallback, trust_env=False, or that proxies passed explicitly keep priority via setdefault. Downstream code that patches get_environ_proxies will also stop affecting this path.
findings.suggestion: Add tests_utils cases: with HTTP_PROXY set and NO_PROXY covering the host, resolve_proxies returns no env proxy; with ALL_PROXY only, the 'all' value is used; trust_env=False ignores the environment; an explicit proxies dict overrides the environment value.
